God swears by the star when it falls, meaning when it sets, that your companion Muhammad ﷺ has neither strayed from the path of truth nor fallen into error. The commentators explain that straying (ḍalāl) is failing to find the right way, while error (ghayy) is holding a false belief and clinging to it. The meaning of the star is disputed. Al-Tabari reports that Mujahid and Ibn Abbas understood it as the Pleiades when they set at dawn, while al-Hasan took it to mean the stars in general. Ibn Kathir cites al-Dahhak, who identifies it with the shooting stars hurled at devils, an interpretation he considers plausible. Mujahid also said it refers to the Quran as it was sent down in stages, and al-Suddi thought it was Venus. As for the falling, most take it as setting, while others take it as the scattering of the stars on the Day of Judgment. The commentators agree on the main point: the Prophet does not speak out of desire, and what he conveys is revelation. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that calling him "your companion" reminds the Quraysh that they know him well and have no grounds for accusing him. Several exegetes, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, also discuss the vision of Gabriel in his true form near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the scholars differ over whether the Prophet saw his Lord, a question that Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas, Aisha and others.

This verse affirms that the Prophet ﷺ does not speak out of personal desire, and that what he conveys is a revelation sent to him by God. The commentators agree on this core meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God revealed to Gabriel, who revealed to the Prophet, and Ibn Kathir cites hadiths to show that he conveys only what has been revealed to him. Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi specify that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, while Ibn al-Qayyim, citing al-Shafi'i, holds that the Sunna is also revelation. Al-Shinqiti draws from the verse the question of whether the Prophet practised independent reasoning, and resolves it by saying that his judgment was itself guided by inspiration. Al-Baghawi and al-Mawardi explain it as meaning he does not speak falsehood, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes that reasoning that comes from revelation may be ascribed to it. Regarding the one of great strength who taught him, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari name Gabriel, though al-Mawardi reports that al-Hasan attributed the teaching to God. On the verses that follow, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy identify the figure with Gabriel, while al-Razi focuses on the distinction between error and moral deviation. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima held that the Prophet saw his Lord, a view Aisha rejected and the majority did not accept.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that what the Prophet ﷺ speaks, which most of them take to be the Qur'an, does not come from his own desire but is a revelation that God inspires in him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi take the pronoun 'it' to refer to the Qur'an, and the revelation to reach the Prophet through Gabriel. Others, such as al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim, hold that the phrase covers everything the Prophet said, so that the Sunna is also part of the revelation, and they support this with transmitted reports. Al-Qasimi disagrees, arguing that the verse does not rule out ijtihad when God permits it. The commentators agree that revelation is divine speech conveyed secretly and swiftly, and that the teacher is Gabriel, according to Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi and Ibn Kathir. Al-Hasan attributes the teaching to God himself, a view Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan find weak. The passage introduces the description of Gabriel's coming, which many say the Prophet saw in his true form twice. Opinions differ on whether God was seen: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ikrima affirm it, while Aisha, Ibn Masud and most scholars deny it. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith 'I only say what is true'.

The commentators explain that the pronoun in « عَلَّمَهُ » refers either to the revelation or to the Prophet ﷺ, and that « شَدِيدُ الْقُوَى » means Gabriel for most of them, as al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi report. Al-Tabari notes that « al-quwa » is the plural of « quwwa », meaning strength and capacity. Al-Hasan al-Basri, by contrast, takes the teacher to be God Himself, a view few others share. For « ذُو مِرَّةٍ », Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada speak of a fine appearance and a tall, handsome build, while Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan take it to mean power. Al-Tabari prefers to understand « mirra » as soundness of body and freedom from defects. Accounts of Gabriel's might are numerous: he is said to have uprooted the cities of Lot's people, lifted them and overturned them, and to have cried out against Thamud, as al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi relate.

On « فَاسْتَوَى », al-Tabari and al-Farra' understand Gabriel as the subject and « وَهُوَ » as the Prophet ﷺ, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Mawardi report that Gabriel appeared in his true form on the upper horizon, filling it. Ibn Kathir holds that the first vision was on earth and the second near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. On « ثُمَّ دَنَا فَتَدَلَّى », most name Gabriel as the one who drew near, while Ibn 'Abbas and Anas attribute it to God, and others to Muhammad approaching his Lord. On « قَابَ قَوْسَيْنِ », Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' take it as the length of two bows, while Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it as two cubits.

On « مَا كَذَبَ الْفُؤَادُ مَا رَأَى », Aisha and Ibn Mas'ud hold that the one seen was Gabriel, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima that the Prophet saw his Lord, while Abu Dharr and Masruq say he saw Him with his heart and not his eyes. Ibn Kathir observes that these questions have been debated for a long time.

The commentators explain that this verse praises the angel who brought the revelation to the Prophet ﷺ, describing him as mighty in power, that is, strong in carrying out what God commands. On the meaning of « dhu mirra », opinions differ: Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to mean a fine appearance and a graceful form, while Mujahid and others take it to mean strength, and Qutrub, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur understand it as soundness of judgment and firmness of mind. Ibn Kathir sees no contradiction between these meanings. As for « fastawa », most exegetes, including Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Kathir, understand that it refers to Gabriel who stood in the highest horizon in his true form. Ibn Jarir held that the pronoun refers to both Gabriel and the Prophet, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari spoke of Gabriel appearing in his true form rather than the forms he usually took. The highest horizon is generally identified with the eastern side, where the sun rises. The drawing near and descending mean that Gabriel came close to the Prophet until the distance was that of two bow-lengths, which some, like al-Razi, take as nearness of rank rather than of place. Opinions also differ on who revealed in « fa-awha ila 'abdihi ma awha »: most say God revealed to His servant Muhammad through Gabriel, while others say Gabriel revealed to the Prophet what God had revealed to him. Regarding the seeing in « ma kadhaba al-fu'ad ma ra'a », Ibn Abbas and Ikrima say the Prophet saw his Lord, while A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Kathir and most scholars say it was Gabriel in his true form.

The commentators explain this verse as part of the description of the angel who taught the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ, which most identify as Jibril. The meaning is that he stood at the highest horizon, the part of the sky facing the observer, which some identify with the horizon where the sun rises. Most take the pronoun "he" to refer to Jibril, while others, such as al-Tabari's sources, take it to refer to the Prophet, so that both stood together at that horizon. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain the highest horizon as the place where the sun rises or where day comes from, while others simply take it as the upper sky. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the verb "stood" can mean that he appeared in his true form, the one in which he was created and which the Prophet saw twice, or that he rose up. The commentators agree that the first vision took place on earth at the highest horizon, and the second in the heavens near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. On the phrase "of strong form", al-Tabari holds it means bodily soundness free from defects, supporting this with a hadith, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Zayd understand strength, and al-Razi adds beauty of appearance and soundness of mind. The commentators do not settle these differences.

The commentators explain that the angel who taught the Prophet the revelation, identified by most as Jibril, drew near and then came down toward him until he was at the distance of two bow-lengths or closer, and then revealed to him what he revealed. Most agree that the subject of "drew near" and "came down" is Jibril: al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas explain the approach as the angel's coming toward the Prophet, with the descent as the bringing of the revelation. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note an inversion in the wording, since descent and approach imply each other. As for "qaba qawsayn", al-Hasan and Qatada take it as the measure of two bows, Ibn Mas'ud as two cubits, and Mujahid as the space between the string and the grip, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as an image of extreme closeness.

Others attribute the approach to God Himself, relying on reports from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas about the night journey. Ibn Kathir holds that this report concerns a different occasion, while Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Sa'di say that divine nearness is one of rank and favour, not of distance. Mujahid attributes the approach to Jibril toward his Lord, and al-Dahhak to Muhammad toward his Lord, when he bowed in prostration.

Regarding "he revealed to His servant what He revealed", some take the revelation to be from God directly, others from Jibril conveying what God had entrusted to him, and Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari favour the latter reading. "The heart did not lie about what it saw" means the heart did not deny what the eyes saw. Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrima say the Prophet saw his Lord, 'A'isha and Ibn Mas'ud say he saw Jibril in his true form, and Abu Dharr reports that he saw a light. The majority holds that the vision was of Jibril.

This passage of Surat an-Najm describes the approach of the angel Gabriel to the Messenger of God ﷺ, coming so close that he was at the distance of two bows or nearer, before conveying the revelation to him. The commentators agree on the literal sense of this nearness, which affirms the certainty of the revelation received. They differ on who drew near and descended: al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn Abbas in one report hold that it was Gabriel who came down to the Prophet, while others, including Ibn Abbas in another transmission and Anas ibn Malik, understand it to be God Himself, a view that Ibn Kathir regards as a narration relating to a different occasion than the verse. Al-Tabari judges that attributing it to Gabriel fits the context best. On the measure of 'qab qawsayn', Qatada and al-Hasan take it as the space between the bowstring and the grip, Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as one or two cubits, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Farra' as the common measure of an Arab bow. Regarding the vision, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima report that the Prophet saw his Lord, Aisha states that it was Gabriel in his true form, and Abu Dharr reports that he saw Him with his heart and not with his eyes. The commentators also note that Gabriel had six hundred wings and that the Prophet saw him in his true form twice.

The commentators explain that this verse, within the passage describing revelation, states that God revealed to His servant Muhammad ﷺ what He revealed. Most understand that Gabriel conveyed to the Prophet what God had given him. All agree that 'His servant' refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and that leaving the content of the revelation unspecified magnifies it, since its greatness exceeds description. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that al-Hasan, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd, and Qatada, hold that Gabriel delivered to Muhammad what his Lord had revealed to him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr holds that the revelation meant is the reminder of God's favours in Surahs Ad-Duha and Al-Sharh. Others report that Paradise was forbidden to prophets until the Prophet entered it, and to nations until his community enters it. Al-Tabari prefers that Gabriel was the one who revealed, since the context of the surah concerns both the Prophet and Gabriel. Ibn Kathir explains that the drawing near and descent took place on earth before the Night Journey. Al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the antecedent clear. No view is decided over the others; the shared point is that the revelation reached the Prophet beyond any doubt.

This verse states that the Prophet's heart did not deny what his eyes saw; rather it affirmed and held it to be true. The commentators agree that what was seen belongs to the great signs of that night, but they differ on what exactly was seen. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Abu Salih, followed by several early scholars, held that the Prophet saw his Lord, al-Tabari noting that he saw Him with the heart rather than the eyes. Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'isha, Abu Dharr and most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, held that it was Jibril in his true form, seen twice. Al-Hasan said he saw the majesty and greatness of God. 'A'isha rejected the claim that the Prophet saw his Lord, and Abu Dharr reported that the Prophet answered him, "It was light; how could I see it?" Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record these views and explain that the reading with a doubled letter means the heart did not treat what was seen as an illusion. Both readings are accepted, the single-letter reading being the more common. Ibn Kathir dates the first vision to the early days of the prophetic mission and the second to the night of the Ascension.

This verse affirms that the Prophet ﷺ saw what he saw with certain vision, with no doubt mixed into his heart, and it rebukes the disbelievers for disputing with him about what he sees with his own eyes. Commentators differ on the reading of the verb: most read « afatumarunahu », meaning « will you dispute with him », while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read « afatamrunahu », meaning « will you deny ». Many hold that both readings converge, since disputing here amounts to denial. As for what was seen, Ibn Mas'ud, Aisha, Abu Dharr and Abu Hurayra, and al-Tabari, say it was Gabriel in his original form, whereas Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and others report that the Prophet saw his Lord, with the heart or with the eyes, a view others reject, and Aisha denied it outright. On the Lote Tree of the Boundary, most identify it as a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, beyond which the knowledge of creatures ends, and some explain what covered it as golden moths, angels or divine light. The Garden of Refuge is for some the garden where martyrs dwell, for others the paradise promised to the righteous. All stress the Prophet's steadfastness in that place: his gaze neither wavered nor went beyond what he was shown.

This passage of Surat al-Najm reports that the Prophet ﷺ saw Gabriel in his true form, the form in which he was created, a second time, near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, a jujube tree in the seventh heaven according to most, or the sixth according to others; it is the point where what ascends from the earth and what descends from above both end, and beside it lies the Garden of Refuge. The commentators broadly agree that the pronoun in 'he saw him' refers to Gabriel, and that 'another descent' means another time of descending. Ibn Abbas and those who followed him held that the Prophet had seen his Lord, by the heart or by the eyes, while A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Dharr denied this and affirmed that what was seen was Gabriel; Ibn Kathir considers this latter view the sound one, given the context. Regarding the verb 'will you dispute with him', the majority reading takes it as disputing, whereas Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it as denying. The commentators report that the polytheists disputed the account of the night journey. As for what covered the lote tree, some said golden moths, others angels, others the light of the Lord, without a firm decision. Most take the greatest signs of God to be the wonders of His dominion, while others describe a vast green silk covering the horizon.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Prophet's second sighting of Gabriel in his true form, near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), a jujube tree in the heavens beyond which no creature passes, and near which lies the Garden of Refuge. Most of them agree that the tree was covered by a divine matter whose details are not fully described. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, Mujahid and Ibrahim said it was a golden moth, while al-Hasan and al-Rabi' spoke of the light of the Lord or of angels gathering around it like crows on a tree. As for the Garden of Refuge, al-Hasan identified it with the paradise promised to the righteous, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada held that it is where the souls of martyrs take refuge, and 'Ata' transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the abode of Gabriel and the angels. On the reason for the name, the scholars offer several explanations: according to Ka'b, the knowledge of all creatures ends at this tree; according to Ibn Mas'ud, whatever ascends from earth and descends from above is received there; according to al-Rabi' ibn Anas, all who follow the Prophet's way reach it. Al-Tabari judged that all these explanations are possible and that no report decisively favours one over another. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also record that Ibn 'Abbas held the Prophet saw his Lord that night, whereas 'A'isha rejected this and maintained that the one seen was Gabriel, the view of most scholars.

This verse states that the Garden of Refuge lies beside the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, a lote tree in the heavens. Most commentators understand it as the garden where the righteous abide, or where the souls of martyrs take shelter. Al-Hasan takes it to be the garden promised to believers, while Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, in one report, hold that it is a separate garden where martyrs' souls dwell, not the promised garden of bliss. 'Ata' transmits from Ibn 'Abbas that it is where Gabriel and the angels take refuge, and Muqatil and al-Kalbi say the same. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also cite Ibn 'Abbas, placing it to the right of the Throne as the abode of the martyrs.

Scholars differ on the meaning of the word al-ma'wa itself. Most take it as the name of a place, while al-Kalbi understands it as the final destination. Some readers recited the word as jannahu, with a pronoun, meaning that the night had covered him; 'A'isha and her companions rejected this reading, though others accepted it as valid.

Most commentators agree that Gabriel was descending to the Prophet in his true form, and that the second sighting took place at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. For the earlier sighting, the majority attribute it to Gabriel, while Ibn 'Abbas and others hold that the Prophet saw his Lord with his heart; 'A'isha denies this. Others speak of a sight with the eyes or the heart, and the commentators do not settle on a single preferred view.

This passage of Surat al-Najm describes the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary during the Night Journey. The commentators explain that the Prophet ﷺ saw Gabriel in his true form a second time near this lote tree, a jujube tree in the heavens, and that the Garden of Refuge is beside it. As for what covered the tree, the verse leaves it unspecified out of majesty. Ibn Mas'ud says it was a golden flying insect, al-Hasan says it was the light of the Lord, and Muqatil says angels settled upon it like crows on a tree. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the Prophet's gaze neither wandered nor overstepped, which shows his perfect conduct in that station. The phrase about seeing the greatest of his Lord's signs is explained by Ibn Mas'ud as a vast green carpet filling the horizon, and by Ibn Zayd as Gabriel in his form in the heavens.

The commentators agree that the sight in question is of Gabriel, that the lote tree is in the heavens, and that what covered it is a great thing no description can capture. They differ on the meaning of the first and second sightings. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra and 'Ikrima hold that the Prophet saw his Lord with his heart, while 'A'isha and Ibn Mas'ud deny this and say it was Gabriel. Abu Dharr reports the answer "a light, how could I see it?", and al-Razi finds the identification of the covering as golden locusts without firm evidence. On the name of the tree, the views vary: it is where the knowledge of creatures ends, where what rises from earth ends, or where what descends from above ends.

The commentators explain that the verse means the Prophet's gaze neither swerved to the right or left from what he saw, nor went beyond what he was commanded to see, but affirmed it with full certainty; this praises the perfection of his conduct at that station. Many agree that the following verses describe the Prophet seeing Gabriel in his true form twice: once at the highest horizon and once near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, a view reported by A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra and upheld by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list several possible meanings, and al-Zamakhshari stresses the precision of the vision. Ibn 'Abbas held that the Prophet saw his Lord, with his eyes or his heart, and cited this verse for it; others, such as A'isha and Abu Dharr, rejected this and said he saw only a light, which is the main point of disagreement. On the 'greatest sign' of his Lord, opinions differ: a vast green carpet filling the horizon according to Ibn Mas'ud, Gabriel in his form according to Ibn Zayd, or all the signs he saw that night according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. The passage thus affirms the truth of the revelation against those who dispute it.

This passage of Surat al-Najm states that the Prophet ﷺ saw, among the greatest signs of his Lord, things that display God's majesty and power. The commentators differ on what these signs were. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and several successors take them to be the vision of Gabriel in his true form: the Prophet saw him twice, once on the higher horizon and once near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, with six hundred wings that filled the horizon. Ibn Mas'ud adds that he saw a green rafraf from Paradise filling the sky. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report that others understood the signs to mean God's signs in general. The commentators agree that the phrase 'his gaze did not swerve nor transgress' praises the Prophet's conduct in that station, since he neither looked right or left nor went beyond what he was shown.

The question of seeing God divides them. Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima report that the Prophet saw his Lord, while 'A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Dharr deny this and say he saw a light or Gabriel. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim lay out this disagreement without deciding between the views, while Ibn Kathir and most later exegetes hold that the vision in the verse is of Gabriel.

There is agreement that the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, or the sixth according to some, beside the Garden of Refuge. They differ on why it is so named: some say it is because the knowledge of creatures ends there, others because what ascends from the earth ends there, and others that it marks the limit beyond which nothing can pass.

In this verse God questions the polytheists about the three idols they worshipped alongside Him: Al-Lat, Al-Uzza and Manat. The commentators explain that the question is a rebuke and a belittling: how can stones and trees be associated with God when guidance has come to them? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that these idols were well known and had shrines and guardians. According to most, Al-Lat stood at Ta'if among the Thaqif, though Ibn Zayd places it at Nakhla near Quraysh. Al-Uzza was honoured by Ghatafan, Quraysh and Banu Kinana, and was described as a tree or a building in different accounts, while Manat stood near Qudayd between Mecca and Medina and was revered by the Aws and Khazraj. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya also mention that some read Al-Latt with a doubled consonant, attributed to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, which would refer to a man who mixed sawiq for pilgrims and was worshipped after his death. The commentators note that describing Manat as the third and the other either adds emphasis or expresses contempt. They largely agree that the verse denies these idols any power and shows they are only names without reality, and that worshipping them rests on conjecture and the desires of the soul rather than any proof from God.

God addresses the polytheists with a rhetorical question about three idols they worshipped: al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, the third in their order of veneration. The commentators agree that these idols have neither benefit nor harm, and that the aim is to belittle them and expose the absurdity of worshipping them. On their locations, opinions differ: Qatada and Ibn Abbas place al-Lat in Ta'if among Thaqif, Ibn Zayd places it at Nakhla among the Quraysh, and Abu 'Ubayda says all three stood inside the Ka'ba; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan favour Ta'if for al-Lat. Mujahid describes al-Uzza as a tree of the Ghatafan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr as a white stone, and al-Kalbi and Ibn Ishaq relate how Khalid ibn al-Walid destroyed it. Manat was a rock of the Hudhayl and Khuza'a near Qudayd between Mecca and Medina, according to most.

Readers also differ on the pronunciation of al-Lat: the majority read it with a light taa, while Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih read it with a doubled taa, explaining it as a man who kneaded sawiq for pilgrims and was worshipped after his death; al-Tabari prefers the single-taa reading as the consensus of the cities. On pausing, some read a final ha and others a taa, following the script of the Mushaf.

The commentators agree on the meaning of "Is the male for you and the female for Him?", that is, how can they attribute daughters to God while keeping sons for themselves. They differ on the "unjust division": Mujahid says crooked, Qatada and Ibn Abbas say unjust, Sufyan says diminished, and Ibn Zayd says contrary. The verse thus rejects the claim that the angels and the idols are daughters of God.

This verse rebukes the polytheists who attributed daughters to God while keeping sons for themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain it as: do you have the males and He the females you dislike, so this is an unjust division. The commentators agree that the rebuke targets the filiation they ascribed to God, whether they regarded the angels or the idols as His daughters. They also agree that the word 'dayza' means unjust, deficient or unequal. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya note the two readings with and without hamza and the grammarians' discussion of its form. On the idols themselves, opinions differ: al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi place al-Lat at Ta'if or Nakhla depending on the report, Qatada places al-Uzza at Nakhla while others describe it as a tree or a white stone, and Manat is located between Mecca and Medina according to some sources. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi conclude that the whole passage shows these names to be empty of reality. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur read 'tilka' as referring to the division itself, and Ibn 'Ashur treats the question as a mocking rhetorical one.

This verse describes the division the polytheists made, assigning daughters to God and sons to themselves, and calls it an unjust and unbalanced division. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain the word "dayza" as unjust; Mujahid and Muqatil say crooked, Sufyan says deficient, Ibn Zayd says contrary, and al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin say unbalanced and unequal. The general sense is that it is absurd to attribute to God what they themselves dislike, and the demonstrative "that" refers to the attribution mentioned just before. The commentators agree that the passage aims to expose the worship of al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, which are mere names invented by the people and their fathers without any authority from God. Al-Tabari and those after him report the views of the grammarians on the form of the word: some explain it as fu'la with a kasra to keep the yaa, as in "bid", while others take a different view. Ibn Kathir notes the reading "dizâ" with a hamza, Abu 'Amr and others read it without, and Zayd ibn 'Ali reads it with a fatha on the dad. The scholars also differ on what the idols were: al-Lat is described as a stone at Ta'if, a tree, or a man who kneaded sawiq for pilgrims, al-'Uzza as a tree among Ghatafan or a white stone, and Manat as a rock near Qudayd. These differences in identification do not change the general judgement against polytheism. The commentators conclude that such beliefs rest on conjecture and desire, while true guidance has come to them from their Lord.

This verse states that the deities worshipped by the idolaters, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, are only names that they and their fathers invented, and that God sent down no authority for them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these idols were venerated by Thaqif, Quraysh, Khuza'a, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, and that the names were supposedly derived from God's own names. The verse also rebukes the attribution of daughters to God while they dislike daughters for themselves. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take the pronoun 'hiya' to refer to the idols themselves, whereas al-Razi and al-Alusi take it to refer to the invented names, with the rebuke remaining the same either way. On the word 'zann', al-Tabari understands it as the assumption that their path is right, and Ibn 'Atiyya defines it as an inclination without proof, while al-Razi notes that certainty was within their reach. On 'dayza', Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada render it as unjust, Sufyan as diminished and Mujahid as crooked. Most commentators take 'al-huda' to mean the guidance brought by the Prophet and the Book, though al-Razi adds the miracles. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn 'Ashur stress that guidance had come and was neglected in favour of desires. Finally, the verse closes the door on vain hopes: intercession benefits only when God permits it and is pleased with the one who receives it.

The commentators explain that this verse rebukes anyone who thinks he will receive whatever he wishes and desires. Everything belongs to God, in this world and the next: He gives to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills, and no one possesses anything in either realm except by His permission. Most of them, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya, understand the wish as the hope of the polytheists that the idols would intercede for them with God. The verse answers that intercession avails only with God's permission and approval, and that even the noble angels intercede only for those He authorises, all the more so the idols. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya mention other readings: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's claim that he will be given wealth and children, another man's claim that he will have the best reward with God, or the wish of some to be prophets. Ibn Juzayy prefers to keep the wording general. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd, also allows that the Prophet ﷺ may have wished for this honour and received it by God's grace. Al-Sam'ani distinguishes a wish, a desire that action does not confirm, from a resolve, which action confirms. Modern commentators such as Ibn 'Uthaymin, Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress that wishes are not fulfilled merely by wanting them, since God controls what happens.

This verse states that the Hereafter and this world both belong to God alone, so a person does not simply get whatever he wishes. Commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that all dominion and command belong to God, and that the idolaters' hopes of intercession through their idols are vain. Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari also take the 'man' to possibly mean the Prophet, who did not gain his honour merely by wishing, but by God's grace, or who wished for it and was granted it. Most exegetes read the word generally and see the verse as answering the polytheists who wanted the benefits of idols' intercession or of having sons. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi list several possible referents for 'what he wished': the intercession of the idols, Walid ibn al-Mughira's claim that he would receive wealth and children, or some people's wish to be prophets. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that God gives prophethood and intercession to whom He wills and approves, not to whoever desires them. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur see the verse as condemning every desire that turns people away from truth, and note that competing wishes cannot all be fulfilled. On the placing of the Hereafter first, Abu Hayyan and al-Biqa'i explain it by the rhyme or by the nature of the idolaters' hopes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that intercession benefits only with God's permission and approval.

This verse states that intercession is of no use before God unless He grants permission and is pleased with the one for whom it is made. The commentators explain that even the angels, who are numerous and close to God in the heavens, cannot benefit anyone through their intercession unless God permits a particular angel to intercede and is pleased with the person being interceded for. Most exegetes read the verse as a rebuke to the pagans who worshipped idols, hoping they would bring them near to God; if the angels are not heard without permission, the idols certainly are not. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take this reading, and Ibn Kathir cites parallel verses from al-Baqara and Saba. The two conditions, divine permission for the intercessor and divine approval of the one interceded for, are repeated by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Uthaymin, among others. Al-Razi notes that the word "kam" signifies a great number, which explains why the singular "malak" is followed by a plural pronoun, and he adds that the verse also brings good news to believers, since the angels ask forgiveness for those on earth. Ibn 'Ashur reads the permission as a willingness to accept, and links the phrase "for whom He wills" to the intercession itself. The verse belongs to a passage that criticises pagan beliefs and affirms that the hereafter and this world belong to God alone.

This verse condemns those who do not believe in the Hereafter for naming the angels with feminine names, because they claimed the angels were daughters of God. It states that they have no knowledge of this and follow only conjecture, which can never replace the truth. The commentators identify them as the pagan Arabs who worshipped idols and hoped for the angels' intercession. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat the claim as a lie and slander without any valid basis, and Ibn Kathir adds that conjecture cannot stand in for truth. Al-Zamakhshari explains that calling the angels daughters amounts to naming each one of them a daughter. Al-Razi traces the belief to a mistaken inference from the feminine ta' in the word for angels, which he rejects, while Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a scornful rebuke of beliefs whose absurdity is clear. Al-Sa'di links the disbelief in the Hereafter to their boldness in such claims. Most exegetes then connect the verse to the command to the Prophet to turn away from those who reject the remembrance and seek only the worldly life, since God knows best who strays and who is guided. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi report that this command is abrogated by the verse of the sword, though not all commentators accept this.

This verse condemns those who do not believe in the Hereafter and who give the angels feminine names, claiming they are the daughters of God. They have no knowledge of this and follow only conjecture, which can never replace the truth. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, agree that the target is the pagan Arabs and that the verse refutes their belief. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the knowledge meant is firm and certain knowledge, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that conjecture is the most false of speech. Al-Razi lists several readings of the pronoun in « by it », which may refer to the saying, the naming, or the angels. He distinguishes practical matters, where conjecture is accepted, from belief, where it is not enough. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani note that the word « truth » here means certain knowledge. Ibn 'Ashur specifies that the conjecture meant is a mistaken opinion. Ibn 'Uthaymin separates baseless conjecture from probable conjecture, which may guide action. As for the rest of the passage, most commentators, among them al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, say the Prophet must turn away from those who turn away from the reminder, meaning the Quran. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that some consider this abrogated by the verse of the sword, but al-Razi finds this view unsound, since turning away fits with the call to fight. Finally, God knows best who goes astray and who is guided.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from those who have turned their backs on His remembrance, meaning the Qur'an or faith, and whose only aim is the life of this world. Commentators explain this turning away as ceasing to argue with them and no longer caring about their fate, not as abandoning the reminder itself. They agree that the verse addresses the Quraysh who denied resurrection and claimed, without knowledge, that the angels were God's daughters; their following of this was mere conjecture, which can never replace the truth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the turning away as a severance and a leaving, while Ibn 'Ashur sees it as indifference to their salvation rather than an end to preaching. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Razi rejects this, arguing that the command to turn away fits with the verses on fighting and cannot be abrogated by them. As for the phrase about the limit of their knowledge, al-Razi takes it to mean either conjecture or the preference for this life, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn relate it to the pursuit of worldly gain. The commentators conclude that God knows best who strays from His path and who is guided, and that He will repay each person according to their deeds.

In this verse God explains that the knowledge of the polytheists who deny the Hereafter reaches no further than worldly affairs, and that their claim that the angels are females was not based on certainty but on conjecture, which is of no use against the truth. God then commands His Prophet to turn away from one who turns from His remembrance and seeks only the life of this world, and reassures him that his Lord knows best who strays from His way and who is guided, and will repay each according to his deeds. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the verse concerns the Arab idolaters who denied resurrection, and understand "that" as referring to their preference for the present life over the Hereafter, with God alone knowing both groups. Ibn 'Atiyya and others hold that the command to turn away was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi argues it simply means ceasing debate after delivering the message, with no abrogation involved. Al-Farra' sees "that" as the measure of their intellect, which goes no further than preferring this world to the next, whereas al-Razi takes it to refer to their reliance on conjecture. Ibn Kathir also cites a transmitted supplication asking that this world not become our greatest concern or the limit of our knowledge. Modern scholars such as Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri stress that God's knowledge encompasses past, present and future, and that the verse warns against misguidance while encouraging guidance.

This verse states that God owns everything in the heavens and on earth, and that He repays each person for their deeds: He will requite those who did evil for what they did, and reward those who did good with the best reward, which is Paradise. The commentators explain that the good-doers are those who avoid the major sins and gross immoralities, and that if they commit minor faults, God forgives and covers them. Most understand the word al-lamam as minor sins, with the exception being disconnected from what precedes it. Al-Tabari holds that it refers to what falls short of fornication, or what lies between the two limits, meaning what carries no legal punishment in this life and no torment in the next. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, Masruq and al-Sha'bi interpret it as a glance, a kiss, and whatever falls short of fornication, while Mujahid and al-Hasan take it as a sin committed once and then repented without relapse. Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Aslam link it to what happened in the pre-Islamic period. Others take it as a passing thought or inclination. As for the command not to praise yourselves, it forbids boasting of one's purity, since God knows best who fears Him. The exegetes also note that God has known people since He created them from earth and while they were embryos, and that this passage answered Jews who declared their dead children to be saints.

This verse describes those who do good as the ones who avoid major sins and gross indecencies, and it reminds us that God repays each person by their deeds: evil with punishment, good with reward. The main debate concerns the exception "except for lamam". Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat it as a detached exception: lamam means minor sins, which prayers and avoiding major sins expiate, a view attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra and al-Sha'bi. Mujahid, al-Hasan and one report from Ibn Abbas understand it as committing a sin, such as fornication or theft, and then repenting without repeating it. Ibn Abbas is also reported to have said it lies between the two limits, the worldly prescribed penalty and the punishment of the hereafter. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi record other views: that lamam is the thought of a sin without acting on it, a passing glance, or the sins of the pre-Islamic period. Ibn Ashur sees the exception as a reassurance to believers. The commentators agree on the vastness of God's forgiveness, on His knowledge of people since Adam's creation and while they were fetuses in the womb, and on the prohibition of praising oneself, since only God knows who is truly pious.

In this verse God addresses the Prophet about a man who turned away from faith, gave a little of his wealth, then stopped and withheld the rest of what he had promised. The commentators agree on the plain sense: turning away from the truth, combined with stinginess and the cutting off of giving. The question is a rebuke and an expression of wonder at such conduct. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who was reproached by a polytheist for abandoning his ancestors' religion, and who agreed to give money in exchange for the other man bearing his punishment in the Hereafter, then grew miserly with the rest. Al-Mawardi and others name other people, such as al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Abu Jahl. Al-Zamakhshari reports a story about Uthman ibn Affan, which Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn Ashur reject as baseless and unworthy of his station. On the word akda, the lexicographers agree it means to stop short, as a digger does when he strikes hard rock. On the phrase 'has he knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees', Ibn Abbas and others take it to mean he sees his fate in the Hereafter, al-Kalbi takes it to mean he knows the Qur'an is true, and al-Zajjaj takes it to mean he sees the lifting of his sin. The passage then recalls what the scrolls of Moses and Abraham contain: no soul bears another's burden, and a person has only what he strove for, a theme tied to divine justice.

The commentators read this verse as describing a man who turned away from faith, gave a small amount, and then stopped. Most take the sense to be that his gift was meagre before it was cut off. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ikrima explain "akda" as cutting off one's giving after a little, and Ibn Kathir compares it to diggers who strike a hard rock and stop.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who promised a polytheist that he would bear the punishment of the Hereafter in exchange for money, and then withheld the rest. Others name al-'As ibn Wa'il, Abu Jahl or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Al-Qurtubi and others mention a tradition about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, which Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan reject as baseless and unworthy of 'Uthman.

On the question "Does he possess knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?", Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as a rebuke. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba understand it as knowledge of his fate in the Hereafter, al-Zajjaj as seeing that his burden is lifted, and al-Kalbi as certainty that the Qur'an he received is true.

The commentators then link this passage to the principle that follows: no one bears another's burden and a person has only his own striving. Ibn 'Abbas held this ruling abrogated by the verse on believing descendants, but most scholars, including Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir, regard it as still in force and treat exceptions as established by other evidence. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Shafi'i drew from it the view that reciting the Qur'an does not reach the dead.

The verse asks whether a man who turned away from faith, gave a little and then stopped, has knowledge of the unseen that would let him see someone else bearing his burden. The implied answer is no, so his guarantee is empty. The commentators agree that a specific person is meant but differ on who he was. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, name al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; as-Suddi names al-As ibn Wa'il; ad-Dahhak names an-Nadr ibn al-Harith; Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi names Abu Jahl. Al-Wahidi and az-Zamakhshari report a story about 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, but Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi call it baseless and unworthy of him. The word 'akda' is generally taken to mean stopping giving, like a digger who strikes hard rock and must halt; Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read it as obedience that was brief and then ended. On 'fa-huwa yara', al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba take it as seeing his state in the hereafter, al-Kalbi as being convinced that what he did is true, and az-Zajjaj as seeing the lifting of his sin. The next verses mention the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim. The commentators say Ibrahim 'fulfilled' what he was commanded, without agreeing on the details. All keep the central principle: no soul bears another's burden, and a person has only what he strove for.

In this verse God asks, in a tone of rebuke, whether the man who turned away after giving a little has knowledge of the unseen so that he sees what he has done. He then asks whether he has not been told what is in the scrolls of Moses, meaning the Torah, and of Abraham, who fulfilled what was required of him and delivered his Lord's message. The commentators agree that the central teaching of these scrolls is that no one bears another's burden and that a person has only what he strives for. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who had promised a man to bear his punishment in the Hereafter in exchange for money, then withheld the rest. Others name al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl or Uthman ibn Affan, though al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya reject the account about Uthman. On the meaning of 'wafa' (fulfilled), opinions differ: al-Hasan, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand it as carrying out what he was commanded and delivering the message, Mujahid as fulfilling what was obligatory on him, and Ibn Abbas as completing all the laws of Islam, which al-Tabari prefers for its general scope. Others point to his willingness to sacrifice his son or to the four morning prayers. On the final clause, Ibn Abbas holds that 'man has only what he strives for' was abrogated by the verse on descendants, while the majority consider it firm. Ikrima restricts it to the peoples of Abraham and Moses, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya affirm that a person benefits from others' deeds, such as charity and supplication, and al-Shafi'i and his followers hold that the recitation of the Quran does not reach the dead.

This verse describes Abraham as the one who « fulfilled » his duty, that is, who carried out fully what he was commanded. The commentators differ on what this fulfilment consisted of. Al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understood it as acting on God's commands and conveying His messages faithfully to his people, Mujahid as performing what was obligatory for him, al-Rabi' as fulfilling his vision by readying to sacrifice his son, and Ibn 'Abbas as carrying out all the precepts of Islam. According to 'Ikrima and al-Hudhayl, Abraham was the first to break with the custom of holding a man accountable for others' sins, proclaiming that no bearer of burdens bears another's burden. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the general reading, complete obedience in all duties, since the text does not restrict the word to one domain. Several reports traced to the Prophet, about four units of prayer at the start of the day or morning and evening remembrances, are cited, but the commentators judged their chains weak. The verse then links to the teaching of the scrolls of Moses and Abraham: no one bears another's burden, and a person gets only what he strove for. Some held this principle abrogated by the verse on the offspring of believers, while most exegetes regard it as binding, while acknowledging that benefit from others' deeds can reach a person through other means.

This passage states that no soul bears the burden of another's sin, a principle the commentators link to the scriptures of Moses and Abraham. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree on this apparent meaning and read it as a refutation of the promise made to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira that another would bear his punishment in the afterlife. Ibn Ashur holds that the negation is general and covers worldly affairs as well as the hereafter. As for the phrase that man has only what he strove for, most take it to mean that a person receives reward only for his own deeds. Ibn Kathir considers that the three things that continue to benefit a person after death, a righteous child, ongoing charity and useful knowledge, are themselves products of his own effort. Al-Hasan and others present it as a rule of justice, while Ibn Abbas claimed the verse was abrogated by the verse on the offspring of believers, a view Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi reject, holding the verse to be valid. Al-Alusi explains that the hadith on whoever starts an evil practice does not contradict it, since the sin charged is that of incitement. Al-Sha'rawi favours the view that a person benefits from the deeds of others, whereas Ibn Uthaymin holds that the burden can only be carried by its doer.

This part of the verse states that a person is recompensed only for what he has himself striven to do, that the deeds of others do not benefit him, and that he does not bear another's burden. The commentators agree on the plain sense: judgment and reward are individual, and each person answers for his own actions. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse concerns a man who had agreed to bear, for money, another man's punishment in the Hereafter, and that the revelation cancels such a bargain. The disagreement concerns whether another's deed can benefit the dead. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima held that the verse is abrogated or specific to the law of Abraham and Moses, citing almsgiving and pilgrimage performed for a deceased person. Al-Rabi ibn Anas said the word man refers to the disbeliever, while the believer receives both what he did and what was done for him. Al-Shafi'i and his followers held that the recitation of the Quran does not reach the dead, since it is not their effort, whereas Ahmad ibn Hanbal and several others held that its reward does reach them. The majority regard the verse as firm and leave the detail of what reaches a person from others' deeds to the books of jurisprudence. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also discussed the meaning of the preposition lam in 'for man'.

The commentators explain that this part of the verse means that each person's effort, that is, his deeds good or bad, will be shown to him and revealed on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be repaid with a complete and perfect reward, without any shortfall. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir agree that the pronoun in « yujzāhu » refers back to the effort, and that « al-awfā » means the most complete and perfect. Ibn Kathir adds that good is rewarded with good and evil with evil. Al-Razi, for his part, suggests that a good deed may appear in a beautiful form, or that the verb « to see » may be understood as « to know ». Most of them link this part to the preceding phrase: a person is repaid only for what he himself has done. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi discuss at length whether a deceased person benefits from good deeds done on his behalf. Those who deny it cite this verse, while those who accept it reply that the verse states what belongs to a person by justice, and that what comes to him from others is by God's grace. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the particle « li » in « lil-insan » indicates possession and entitlement. Ibn Kathir does not allow the transfer of the reward for Qur'an recitation, whereas al-Sha'rawi holds that the verse does not forbid benefiting from the deeds of others, and that the effort may be good or bad.

This verse states that a person will be repaid for his striving with a full and complete recompense, with nothing diminished. The commentators explain that "al-jaza' al-awfa" means the most complete and perfect reward. Al-Tabari understands the pronoun in "yujzahu" to refer to the striving (sa'y): a person is rewarded for his action with the fullest of the rewards God has promised. Most exegetes agree on this point: each person is judged by what he has done, with a warning for the disbelievers and good news for the believers, as Ibn 'Atiyya reports.

Al-Razi notes that the word "awfa" implies an excess, so that the reward of the believers may include, beyond Paradise, the vision of God. Opinions differ on the pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud allow that it may refer to the recompense itself, with "al-jaza' al-awfa" serving as its explanation or apposition. Abu Hayyan however notes that this apposition is disputed and he rejects it.

Related to the preceding phrase, "man has only what he strove for," commentators have debated whether one may benefit from the deeds of others. Ibn Kathir holds that the recitation of the Qur'an cannot be offered to the dead, while Ibn al-Qayyim argues that a pious act done by a living person can reach the deceased when it is dedicated to him. Yet all agree on the central idea: divine justice is perfect, and each person answers for his own striving.

The commentators explain that the verse means that the final end, return and destiny of all creatures lies with God alone, who will call them to account and repay them for their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take it to mean the return to God on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi say the word refers to the place of return and the destiny of the servants, while Ibn 'Atiyya widens the meaning to include resurrection, Paradise and Hell. Al-Razi, Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Alusi offer another reading: the reasoning of the mind ends at God, so one should not reflect upon His essence. They cite the report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'no reflection on the Lord', and the saying of Abu Hurayra to reflect on creation rather than on the Creator. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that this report is not preserved in this wording, and Ibn Kathir considers it weak.

The commentators agree in placing the verse within the context of judgement and divine justice, and in seeing the return to God as an unavoidable reality. On recitation, Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that both readings, with the hamza opened or kasra, are sound; he advises against using the less familiar one before people who might be confused. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the word signifies reaching a limit, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the general meaning embraces every form of return.

The commentators explain that God is the One who created laughter and weeping in human beings, as a sign of His power. They differ on the precise meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Kalbi say that He makes the people of Paradise laugh in Paradise and the people of the Fire weep in the Fire, a reading that Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur link to the idea that laughter expresses joy and weeping expresses sorrow. Al-Dahhak understands that He makes the earth laugh with plants and the sky weep with rain, a figurative sense. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it rather to mean that God gladdens whom He wills and saddens whom He wills in this world, a view also given by al-Jalalayn and al-Sa'di. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that He created the faculties of laughing and weeping, which Abu Hayyan finds coloured by Mu'tazili thought. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Uthaymin maintain that laughing and weeping are real acts: God is the Laugher and the Weeper in truth, and the human being truly laughs and weeps. Al-Biqa'i notes that these states are not chosen by the one who experiences them. Ibn 'Ashur observes that a person is never without either joy or sorrow, and that laughter is mentioned before weeping for the sake of the rhyme.

This verse affirms that God alone causes death and gives life: He determines the causes of death and of life, and no one else can do so. The commentators offer several readings. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi say it may mean that He made the fathers die and the sons live, or that He causes death in this world and life for the resurrection. Al-Mawardi, al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur understand death and life in their literal sense, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the order of the words serves the rhyme of the verse. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it that God created death and life. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi report the view that death is unbelief and life is faith, while others see drought and abundance, or sleep and waking. Al-Sha'rawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that a killer or a doctor only brings about the conditions, while the actual death comes from God, and Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that God gives life both in this world and in the Hereafter. The commentators do not choose among these meanings, which they treat as all possible readings of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God created the two sexes, male and female, from a drop of semen that is emitted. Al-Tabari understands that each of the two is a pair for the other, and that the word "min" (from) is linked to the verb "created". Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn take the two sexes to refer to all animals, while al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi report the view of al-Dahhak that the pair is Adam and Eve, which al-Sam'ani considers less sound than the general sense of male and female among the children of Adam. Several interpreters take "nutfa" to mean a small quantity of water, and "tumna" to mean poured into the womb. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash understand it as "decreed", meaning that God determines the child from that drop. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur connect the passage to resurrection: the one who created the first beginning can recreate, and this second creation is the new birth. Ibn Ashur also explains that mentioning the pair points to the fact that each sex contributes a share of the seed. Al-Shinqiti notes that the verse attributes the nutfa to the man, and Ibn Uthaymin stresses that one material produces two sexes with different natures, a sign of divine power. The commentators agree on the general meaning and differ on the scope of the terms.

This verse states that God created the two kinds, male and female, from a drop of semen that is poured forth into the womb, and that the second creation, the raising of the dead, belongs to Him. The commentators have given two main meanings to the word tumna. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ata', take it to mean that the seed is poured out into the womb. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash take it to mean that it is measured out, so that God determines the child from the drop. Ibn Ashur notes that the phrase "when it is poured forth" hints at how quickly formation begins when the two fluids mix, while others regard it as simply a time indicator. Al-Razi suggests that the "other creation" may refer to the breathing of the human spirit into the embryo, whereas most commentators, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand it as the resurrection after death. There is agreement that the first creation is a proof of God's power to bring the dead back to life, and that no one claims a share in it. Ibn Uthaymin adds that the word zawj here means a kind, and that creating the two sexes from one substance shows the perfection of divine power.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that it is God alone who will bring created beings back to life after death, through a second creation for resurrection and recompense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as the gathering of bodies and souls after death, while al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi speak of souls being returned to bodies. The word "al-ukhra" (the second) is taken by al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur to mean that the One who created the first time can create again.

Opinions differ on the sense of "'alayhi" (incumbent upon Him). Most exegetes take it as the fulfilment of a promise, as al-Razi and Ibn 'Uthaymin explain, the latter describing an obligation God places upon Himself. Al-Zamakhshari, by contrast, reads it as a requirement of wisdom so that God may reward good and evil, and al-Alusi and al-Shinqiti criticise this as a Mu'tazilite reading. Al-Razi also proposes that the word marks the certainty of the act.

The reading of "al-nash'a" also varies: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a long vowel, while the majority read it short. Al-Razi notes that the noun expresses the actual realisation of the re-creation. In these commentaries the verse closes the account of the creation of humankind from a drop of emitted semen.

This phrase states that God alone makes people rich and grants them contentment, meaning He gives wealth and provides lasting property that people keep as possessions. The commentators differ on the two verbs. Abu Salih, Ibn Zayd, al-Akhfash and al-Taymi explain them as enriching with wealth and granting an estate, or, in the case of the second verb, impoverishing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the richness is material and that qunya refers to the principal assets kept beyond sufficiency. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand that God gives and satisfies, and that the second verb means He makes one content with what he was given. Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan take the verbs to mean that God makes people clients and provides servants. Ibn Zayd reads it as enriching whom He wills and impoverishing whom He wills. Ibn Kathir also reports a view that God enriched Himself and made creation need Him. Al-Razi notes that enrichment meets need while contentment goes beyond it. Ibn Ashur observes that the separate pronoun restricts the action to God. All agree that provision and wealth belong to God alone.

This verse states that God is the Lord of Sirius (ash-Shi'ra), a bright star that rises after Orion in the heat of summer, and that some Arabs, above all the tribe of Khuza'a, used to worship it besides God. The commentators report that Abu Kabsha, a chief of that tribe, was the first to establish this worship, and that the Quraysh used to call the Prophet ﷺ the son of Abu Kabsha because he opposed their religion. They agree that the star meant is al-'Abur, the brighter of the two Shi'ras, the other being al-Ghumaysa, and they note that it is singled out because its worship was widespread. God thus makes clear that He is its Lord, Owner and Governor, and that it is a created thing and not deserving of worship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate that Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd identified it with the star called Mirzam al-Jawza', while al-Sam'ani reports the view that it is Venus, which he says goes against the apparent meaning of the verse. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the Khuza'a also called it Kalb al-Jabbar, the hunter's dog. Al-Alusi prefers al-'Abur as the most obvious meaning, being larger and brighter. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the spread of star worship in the Hijaz. Al-Jaza'iri, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin conclude that it establishes God's sole lordship and the created nature of the star. No commentator disputes this general sense.

This verse states that God destroyed the first 'Ad, the people of Hud, and commentators explain the epithet "first" in several ways. Most, including Ibn Zayd, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi's circle, take it to mean that they were the most ancient, the first nation destroyed after the people of Noah. All agree that they were destroyed by a fierce, violent wind, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress their great strength and arrogance, which made their punishment all the more striking. The commentators differ on whether there were two 'Ad. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Mawardi report that a branch of 'Ad settled in Mecca with the Amalekites and escaped the punishment, perishing later, which is why they were called the second 'Ad. Ibn Ishaq says that the first 'Ad perished by the wind and the second by the cry. Ka'b al-Ahbar holds that the people of Hud were the second 'Ad, descended from the first, while al-Mubarrad identifies the second 'Ad with Thamud. On recitation, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr assimilate the tanwin into the lam and drop the hamza, while the Kufans pronounce it clearly. Al-Tabari judges the Kufan reading the most eloquent, but accepts both. The verse belongs to a list of destroyed nations, offered as a warning to the Prophet's contemporaries.

This passage of Surat al-Najm states that God destroyed the first 'Ad, the people of Hud, and Thamud, the people of Salih, leaving none of them alive, meaning that both groups were annihilated by His punishment. The commentators explain that this destruction came after these peoples had denied their messengers and persisted in arrogance. The verses then mention the people of Noah, who came before these nations and are described as more wrongful and more rebellious, and the commentators cite the long duration of Noah's preaching among them as evidence. All agree that 'the first 'Ad' refers to the people of Hud, and that the epithet 'first' refers either to their antiquity or to their precedence among the nations; Ibn Zayd and most scholars hold that they were the first nation destroyed after Noah's people. Al-Tabari, however, accepts that another 'Ad existed, settled in Mecca with the Amalekites, a view Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Atiyya reject as unsound. On recitation, the commentators note that the tanwin of 'Adan can be pronounced or dropped and that Thamud is read with or without declension; al-Tabari judges both readings correct, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes the undeclined form to refer to the tribe. The Mu'tafika are identified as the cities of Lot's people, which Gabriel overturned before they were showered with stones, and commentators differ on whether the pronoun in 'then covered them with what covered' refers to the stones or to the whole punishment. The address is to the denier, and the verses are understood as a reminder of God's blessings and of the punishments inflicted on those who rejected Him.

This verse states that Allah destroyed the people of Noah before 'Ad and Thamud, and that they were more wrongdoing and more rebellious than the nations destroyed after them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Noah preached to them for a thousand years minus fifty, and that his call only increased their stubbornness, so that a man would take his son by the hand to warn him against Noah, just as his own father had warned him. The commentators agree that the overturned cities are the towns of the people of Lot, turned upside down with their inhabitants: according to al-Tabari, Gabriel lifted them and then tipped them over, and Allah covered them with stones. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari understand the word 'ahwa' as meaning that they were made to fall. Al-Nasafi and al-Mawardi explain that the people of Noah's excess in wrongdoing lay in the length of his mission and their abuse of him, beating him until he could not move and keeping their children from hearing him. Al-Razi says wrongdoing means placing something where it does not belong, while transgression means going beyond limits, and that transgression is the more severe form of wrongdoing. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur also report the view that the pronoun refers to all the peoples mentioned, which would console the Prophet. Ibn 'Ashur explains that 'Ad al-Ula means the earliest 'Ad, not a second 'Ad. Differences in recitation of 'Adan al-Ula' and 'Thamuda' do not change the meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the list of peoples destroyed by God: al-Mu'tafika refers to the towns of the people of Lot, overturned along with their inhabitants, and 'ahwa' means that God brought them down after raising them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Gabriel lifted them and then turned them over, while al-Razi and al-Alusi note that the word can apply more broadly to any settlement whose dwellings were overturned. Al-Mawardi counts five towns, including Sodom, and Ibn 'Ashur counts four, and the other scholars do not settle the number. All agree that the passage is a warning addressed to the Prophet's contemporaries. Regarding the phrase 'fa-ghashshaha ma ghasha', al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as an amplification that leaves the punishment deliberately undefined. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur report that stones fell from the sky, whereas al-Razi also considers that it refers to the cause of divine anger. The disagreements therefore concern the exact manner of the raising and falling, the number of towns, and who carried out the punishment, not the general meaning of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the list of nations destroyed for rejecting their messengers. It mentions the people of Noah, whom al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe as the most wrongdoing and rebellious, because Noah called them for a very long time, close to a thousand years minus fifty. It then names the overturned cities, al-mu'tafikah, which God turned upside down.

Most exegetes agree that these are the cities of the people of Lot. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd report that Gabriel lifted them and then overturned them, and that stones fell upon them. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi say there were five such cities. Al-Razi notes that the word may also refer to any place whose dwellings were overthrown.

The meaning of what covered them is debated. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand it as stones, while al-Mawardi gives two options, Gabriel or the stones. Al-Razi suggests that God is the subject, or that the cause of His anger is meant. Many, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di, observe that the vagueness is deliberate, to convey terror and immensity.

Finally, the commentators draw the lesson that the listener should not doubt the blessings of his Lord. Ibn Juzayy, al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Uthaymin add that even these punishments are a form of grace, since they offer a lesson, as al-Alusi notes.

God addresses the human being with a rhetorical question of reproach: which of your Lord's blessings will you doubt, dispute or deny? The commentators explain that the word 'ala' means blessings, and that the address is to mankind in general or to the disbeliever in particular, though some direct it to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the punishments described earlier in the surah are also called blessings, since they carry lessons for the reflective and support for the prophets and believers. The verb 'tamara' means to doubt; Ibn 'Abbas renders it as to deny, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy render it as doubt or dispute. Al-Razi holds that doubt cannot be attributed to the Prophet, so the address is general. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a summary conclusion of the blessings listed. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that people should acknowledge these favours and give thanks to God rather than credit causes alone.

This verse declares that this is a warning of the same kind as the earlier warnings, and the commentators differ on what the reference points to. Ibn Jurayj, al-Kalbi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, sent as earlier messengers were sent to their peoples. Qatada, Abu Malik and those who follow them understand it as the Quran, or as the accounts of destroyed nations found in the earlier scriptures of Abraham and Moses. Al-Tabari prefers to link the demonstrative to the preceding passage of the surah, while Ibn 'Ashur explains that a discourse present in the mind may be pointed to as if it were before the eyes. On the general sense, the commentators agree that the warning belongs to the line of prophets who came before.

They also agree that "al-azifa" is the Hour, called near because it draws close to humankind. Only God can reveal it or fix its time, according to Tabari and Zamakhshari, while Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak say no one can turn back its terrors once they overwhelm creation. Al-Razi connects this passage to three successive principles: the oneness of God, the prophetic mission and the resurrection. The word "nudhur" is read as the plural of "nadhir", and the qualifier "the first" is taken as a description of kind rather than a distinction between warnings.

The commentators explain that this verse announces the nearness of the Hour. The verb azifat means that the moment has drawn close and is at hand, and al-Azifa is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the Hour itself, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that it is called near either because its time is close with God or because it draws near to people so that they may prepare. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi cite verses by al-Nabigha and Ka'b ibn Zuhayr to establish the sense of nearness.

Opinions differ on the phrase 'none can reveal it apart from God'. Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and al-Razi understand that only God discloses its time or its reality, whereas 'Ata', Qatada and al-Dahhak read it as meaning that once its terrors overwhelm creation, no one can avert them. Al-Farra' explains that the feminine form functions like a verbal noun, as in al-'afiya, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the feminine ending may also express intensity. As for what 'this' refers to in 'this is a warner', Ibn Kathir, Qatada and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the Prophet, Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean the Qur'an, and Abu Malik takes it to mean the accounts of earlier nations. Al-Tabari judges the last view closest to the context.

The commentators also connect the following verses, which rebuke those who marvel at the Qur'an and mock it with laughter instead of weeping. Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya cite reports encouraging weeping when it is recited. Several commentators note that the surah calls for a prostration of recitation, which most of the scholars cited accept, whereas Malik and Ibn 'Umar did not regard it as an obligatory prostration.

The commentators explain that this verse states that when the Hour, called "the imminent" because it is near, draws close, no one besides God can uncover it, reveal it, or ward it off. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand that its occurrence is revealed only by God's decree, since He alone knows its time, and that neither a near angel nor a sent prophet has been shown it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy give a similar reading, in which "uncovering" means making its time manifest or clear.

Most agree that the Hour is near and that God alone fixes its moment. The feminine form of "kashifa" has prompted several explanations: a verbal noun like "al-'afiya", an adjective implying a soul or a state, or an intensive form. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur, take it to mean disclosing the Hour's timing, while Ibn al-Jawzi also reports Ata', Qatada and al-Dahhak, who hold that no one can remove its terrors once they overwhelm people.

The context is a warning. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say the Prophet is a warner like the earlier ones and that the Hour is close. These same authors then reproach the disbelievers for wondering at and laughing at the Qur'an instead of weeping. On the word "samidun", they cite several meanings: proud, heedless, or engaged in singing, as in the Himyarite dialect. All of them call the listener to prostration and to worship of God.

God rebukes the Quraysh for marvelling at the Qur'an and mocking it with laughter instead of weeping in fear of its warning, while they remain heedless and turn away from it, and then commands them to prostrate and worship Him alone. The commentators agree that "this discourse" refers to the Qur'an, that the wonder expressed is denial and disbelief, and that the laughter is mocking laughter. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also mention a possible reading in which the reference is to the resurrection and recompense described in the preceding verses, so that the wonder concerns the raising of bodies after death. The meaning of "samidun" varies. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean heedless, distracted and turning away; 'Ikrima and Abu 'Ubayda take it as singing in the Himyarite dialect; al-Dahhak and one report from Mujahid understand arrogance and haughtiness; 'Ali and al-Hasan understand standing for prayer before the imam arrives. Ibn al-Qayyim gathers these senses, arguing that singing includes them all. Many scholars draw from the verse a recommendation to weep when reciting the Qur'an, and report that the Prophet was not seen laughing after its revelation. On the prostration of recitation at this verse, most hold it to be prescribed, while Ibn 'Umar and Malik did not accept it and read the command as referring to the prayer prostration. The closing words call for monotheism and humble submission to God.

This verse rebukes the Meccan disbelievers: they marvel at the Qur'an and laugh at it in mockery, and they do not weep at its warnings, while they are heedless and turned away from it. The commentators give the word "sāmidūn" closely related meanings. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and 'Ikrima took it to mean heedless, distracted or turning away. Many report that in the Yemeni dialect the word means singing: when they heard the Qur'an they sang and played to drown it out. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also cite Ibn 'Abbas's sense of haughtiness and pride, Mujahid's sense of scowling with a puffed-up face, and the explanation of 'Ali and al-Hasan that it means standing while waiting for the imam to pray. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that all these meanings come together in singing, play and arrogance. The commentators report that after this verse the Prophet was never seen laughing except with a smile, and they hold that weeping while hearing the Qur'an is recommended, as al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note. On the command to prostrate and worship, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i understand a prostration of recitation, while al-Qurtubi notes that Ibn 'Umar and Malik did not regard it as an obligatory prostration, and Muqatil takes it to mean the five daily prayers. Al-Razi links the command to gratitude for guidance.

In this verse God addresses the Quraysh, who wonder at the Quran, laugh at it and do not weep at its warnings, and tells them: and you are sāmidūn. Most commentators take the word to mean heedless, distracted and turned away from the lessons of the revelation. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report this sense from Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Juzayy and the Tafsir al-Jalalayn give the same meaning.

Other meanings are recorded. Ikrima, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, explains the word as singing in the dialect of Yemen, where people say smud for us, meaning sing for us; the idolaters sang when they heard the Quran to distract people from it. Al-Nasafi mentions this meaning, and Ibn al-Qayyim argues that singing gathers all the other senses. Al-Dahhak reads it as insolent and boastful, Mujahid as angry with swollen lips, and Ibn Abbas, in another report, as lifting the head with pride. Al-Mubarrad takes it as motionless, and Abu al-Su'ud as humble and still.

Some relate the word to standing during prayer. Ali, al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i are reported to have seen people standing and waiting for the imam instead of sitting, and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi cite this reading. Al-Biqa'i instead links it to persistent effort at work, and Ibn Ashur understands it as self-admiration.

After rebuking the disbelievers for mocking the Qur'an and turning away from it, God commands them here to prostrate to Him and worship Him alone, not the idols. The commentators explain the word "samidun", used to describe them, in different ways. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean heedlessness, distraction, aversion and arrogance, and 'Ikrima and Abu 'Ubayda add that in the Himyarite dialect samud means singing: when they heard the Qur'an they sang and played. Al-Hasan, Ibrahim and, by one report, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib understood it as standing for prayer while waiting for the imam to arrive, while al-Mubarrad gave it the sense of being stupefied. All agree on the core idea of neglecting the Qur'an and refusing to listen to it. On the prostration commanded, opinions differ: Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, understand it as the prostration of recitation, which the Prophet performed here together with believers and polytheists, whereas Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar and Malik did not treat it as a required prostration, Ibn 'Umar taking it to refer to the obligatory prayer. Al-Sam'ani reports that some scholars linked it to the five daily prayers. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi present the particle "fa" as a logical consequence of the preceding rebuke, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that the prostration may signify submission and awe, or prayer and entry into Islam, and that the worship meant is pure monotheism.
